L18@P0: Boswell, P. J. Sanchez, D. L. Moulton, L. L. Kitchens, G. J. Rooker, and A. Aschenbrenner. 2018. Seascape connectivity
L19@P0: and the influence of predation risk on the movement of fishes inhabiting a back-reef ecosystem. Ecosphere 9(4):e02200.
L20@P0: 10.1002/ecs2.2200
L21@P0: Abstract. The mangrove–seagrass–patch reef (MSP) ecosystem serves as the principal back-reef nursery
L22@P0: for many reef fishes in the Caribbean, but the functional roles of habitats that form this seascape remain
L23@P0: unclear. We assessed ecosystem and trophic connectivity of two common reef fishes (schoolmaster, Lutjanus apodus; white grunt, Haemulon plumierii) and one predator (great barracuda, Sphyraena barracuda) in a
L24@P0: Caribbean MSP ecosystem using acoustic telemetry and natural dietary tracers. Triangulated positions
L25@P0: from an acoustic positioning system indicated that L. apodus and H. plumierii relied on multiple habitats
L26@P0: within this MSP ecosystem, occupying areas with more cover (lower risk) during the day and areas with
L27@P0: less cover (higher risk) at night. During the day, both species exhibited limited movement away from structured habitats (e.g., mangroves, patch reef) and avoided the primary activity space of S. barracuda in the
L28@P0: central channel over sand bottom or seagrass. At night, L. apodus moved into the channel and adjacent seagrass beds on the margin of this high-risk area when S. barracuda occurrence was reduced, suggesting that
L29@P0: this species adjusts its foraging activities to minimize encounter rates with predators. Haemulon plumierii
L30@P0: also displayed distinct day–night shifts with directed movements at twilight across higher risk habitat to
L31@P0: nighttime locations in seagrass. Conspicuous changes in the rate of movement were also detected at different times of the day, and observed mismatches between movement rates of S. barracuda and our two potential prey species appeared to be a behavioral response to reduce their vulnerability. Dietary tracer analysis
L32@P0: supported the premise that observed shifts to nocturnal habitats were associated with foraging, with significant contributions of organic matter derived from nighttime locations. Findings from this study clearly
L33@P0: demonstrate that the configuration of habitats and spatiotemporal variability in predation risk are key
L34@P0: determinants of movement and foraging activities for these species, indicating that an improved understanding of seascape connectivity is critical to the management of reef-dependent species.
L35@P0: Key words: acoustic telemetry; coral reef; foraging; habitat connectivity; migration; nursery habitat; stable isotopes.

L40@P0-1: ❖ www.esajournals.org 1 April 2018 ❖ Volume 9(4) ❖ Article e02200INTRODUCTION
L41@P1: Marine fishes commonly reside in complex
L42@P1: seascapes, and their population dynamics are
L43@P1: inherently linked to connectivity via movements
L44@P1: at the habitat-, ecosystem-, and/or ocean-basin
L45@P1: scale (Mumby and Hastings 2008, Rooker and
L46@P1: Secor 2005, Rooker et al. 2008, Nagelkerken et al.
L47@P1: 2015). Foraging success and survival of marine
L48@P1: fishes are affected by their differential use of
L49@P1: habitats (Clark et al. 2009, Hammerschlag et al.
L50@P1: 2010), and spatiotemporal shifts are often
L51@P1: assumed to be behavioral adjustments that optimize foraging success and minimize predation
L52@P1: risk (Werner et al. 1983, Lima and Dill 1990).
L53@P1: Given that many marine fishes require or utilize
L54@P1: multiple habitats or ecosystems during ontogeny,
L55@P1: the decline or loss of any component of a seascape can profoundly impact year-class strength
L56@P1: (Dahlgren and Eggleston 2000). In response, an
L57@P1: improved understanding of the causes of spatiotemporal shifts, including those linked to
L58@P1: predator activity, is critically needed to determine the value and functional role of different
L59@P1: components of a seascape.
L60@P1: Predation is a fundamental mechanism regulating the survival and dynamics of prey populations (Werner and Anholt 1993). Predators can
L61@P1: influence the distribution and abundance of prey
L62@P1: directly (consumptive) and indirectly through
L63@P1: behavioral adjustments to predation risk (Trussell et al. 2006, Matassa et al. 2016), and the
L64@P1: threat of predation typically varies in time and
L65@P1: space across heterogeneous marine ecosystems
L66@P1: (Wirsing et al. 2008). Vulnerability of prey within
L67@P1: a seascape or landscape (i.e., terrestrial ecosystems) is determined by both the spatial configuration of the habitat patches and boundaries and
L68@P1: the spatiotemporal distribution of both predators
L69@P1: and conspecifics (Tambling et al. 2012). As a
L70@P1: result, ranging (migration) and foraging behaviors of prey are presumably structured to some
L71@P1: degree by the perceived risk associated with different components of a seascape (Rooker and
L72@P1: Dennis 1991, Hammerschlag et al. 2010).
L73@P1: The mangrove–seagrass–patch reef (MSP)
L74@P1: ecosystem serves as the principal back-reef nursery for a variety of reef-dependent species, and
L75@P1: these shallow water seascapes are increasingly
L76@P1: threatened by coastal development (Mumby
L77@P1: et al. 2004, Nagelkerken et al. 2015). Spatially
L78@P1: diverse assemblages of juvenile fishes within
L79@P1: MSP ecosystems are common, with individuals
L80@P1: frequently crossing multiple habitats or ecotones
L81@P1: on a daily basis (Nagelkerken and van der Velde
L82@P1: 2004, Adams et al. 2006, Nagelkerken et al.
L83@P1: 2008). Spatial shifts by juvenile reef fishes are
L84@P1: commonly assumed to be predator-mediated
L85@P1: responses, with individuals moving between safe
L86@P1: shelter areas of higher habitat complexity and
L87@P1: more precarious open areas with lower complexity. Moreover, the nature and timing of spatial
L88@P1: shifts appear to be influenced by predators, with
L89@P1: prey altering their movements to minimize
L90@P1: encounter rates with predators, following the
L91@P1: “predation risk allocation hypothesis” of Lima
L92@P1: and Bednekoff (1999). While directed habitat
L93@P1: shifts within the MSP ecosystem are common
L94@P1: and known to vary ontogenetically, the most conspicuous and predictable redistribution of fishes
L95@P1: occurs between the day and night during twilight migrations (Helfman 1986, Rooker and
L96@P1: Dennis 1991). Although general characterizations
L97@P1: of diel distributions and habitat connectivity of
L98@P1: juvenile fishes within MSP ecosystems have been
L99@P1: previously published (Nagelkerken et al. 2000,
L100@P1: Appeldoorn et al. 2009), the influence of predation—direct or perceived—on the habitat use
L101@P1: and movement of juvenile reef fishes remains
L102@P1: poorly understood.
L103@P1: The purpose of the current study was to assess
L104@P1: the population connectivity of two reef fishes
L105@P1: that commonly use the MSP ecosystem as nursery habitat: schoolmaster [snapper] (Lutjanus apodus) and white grunt (Haemulon plumierii). We
L106@P1: characterized the movement and habitat use of
L107@P1: juvenile L. apodus and H. plumierii using an
L108@P1: emerging technology (acoustic positioning system) and then related fine-scale movement data
L109@P1: of both species to predation risk by concurrently
L110@P1: tracking a common predator in this MSP ecosystem, great barracuda (Sphyraena barracuda). The
L111@P1: selected MSP ecosystem also included an open
L112@P1: (deep channel with sand bottom) or higher risk
L113@P1: habitat, which allowed us to further assess the
L114@P1: influence of predation risk on both species. In
L115@P1: addition, we incorporated dietary tracer data
L116@P1: (stable isotopes) to investigate the link between
L117@P1: spatiotemporal shifts within the MSP ecosystem
L118@P1: and trophic connectivity for all three species.
L119@P1: Similar to observations of preferential selection
L120@P1: by prey to safer regions of terrestrial landscapes
L121@P1: ❖ www.esajournals.org 2 April 2018 ❖ Volume 9(4) ❖ Article e02200
L122@P1-2: ROOKER ET AL.(Valeix et al. 2009), we hypothesized that habitat
L123@P2: use as well as the timing and magnitude of
L124@P2: trans-boundary movements by L. apodus and
L125@P2: H. plumierii was influenced by the presence of
L126@P2: predators and/or the perceived predation risk
L127@P2: associated with particular habitats or areas.
L128@P2: Given that both species are known to display
L129@P2: conspicuous day–night movements across seascapes, we anticipated that these directed and predictable habitat shifts were related to foraging.
L130@P2: METHODS
L131@P2: Study area
L132@P2: The study was performed in a back-reef seascape in the Guanica Biosphere Reserve located
L133@P2: off the southwestern coast of Puerto Rico (Fig. 1).
L134@P2: The study site included two small mangrove
L135@P2: keys within the Cayos de Cana Gorda and ~
L136@P2: included all habitats typically found within the
L137@P2: MSP ecosystem in the Caribbean: red mangrove
L138@P2: (Rhizophora mangle), seagrass, and patch reefs.
L139@P2: The mangrove keys within the study site were
L140@P2: separated by a deeper channel (Fig. 1) with a
L141@P2: sand bottom and mixed stands of seagrass,
L142@P2: mainly turtle grass (Thalassia testudinum) with
L143@P2: lesser amounts of manatee grass (Syringodium filiforme) and shoal grass (Halodule wrightii) present
L144@P2: from the channel edge to the mangrove prop
L145@P2: roots on each side of the channel. Large stands of
L146@P2: T. testudinum were also present on the leeward
L147@P2: side of each mangrove key in the northwestern
L148@P2: region of the seascape. The southeastern region
L149@P2: of the seascape contained several small patch
L150@P2: Fig. 1. Map of study site in the Guanica Biosphere Reserve located off the southwestern coast of Puerto Rico. Large
L151@P2: inset map shows the spatial configuration of habitats within the mangrove–seagrass–patch reef ecosystem and the
L152@P2: location of receivers (solid circles) in the acoustic positioning system. Bathymetry is also denoted with contour lines.
L153@P2: ❖ www.esajournals.org 3 April 2018 ❖ Volume 9(4) ❖ Article e02200
L154@P2-3: ROOKER ET AL.reefs, comprised primarily of Porites astreoides,
L155@P3: Porites porites, Siderastrea radians, and Siderastrea
L156@P3: siderea.
L157@P3: High-resolution bathymetric and benthic habitat maps were created using both ortho-rectified
L158@P3: aerial imagery and in situ observation. Orthorectified aerial images (resolution 0.3 m; US Army
L159@P3: Corps of Engineers 2006) were used to determine
L160@P3: initial boundaries between habitats within the
L161@P3: study area. The composition and boundary of
L162@P3: each habitat patch were then classified in situ
L163@P3: using a handheld GPS unit to both ground truth
L164@P3: and refine the discrimination of benthic habitats.
L165@P3: Habitats were then digitized in a geographic
L166@P3: information system (ArcGIS 10.2.2, ESRI, Redlands, California, USA) for visualization and
L167@P3: analysis purposes. Bathymetric maps were constructed from in situ depth observations recorded
L168@P3: at 138 locations within the seascape. The majority
L169@P3: of these locations were gridded at approximately
L170@P3: 5-m intervals throughout the study area; however,
L171@P3: locations were also strategically placed in areas of
L172@P3: high bathymetric relief (i.e., channel edges) to
L173@P3: ensure accurate representation of these features.
L174@P3: Depth was then interpolated using ordinary kriging to create a continuous raster surface. Current
L175@P3: measurements taken with a flowmeter (Model
L176@P3: 2030R, General Oceanics, Miami, Florida, USA) at
L177@P3: 15 locations within the seascape were used to classify areas of high or low current velocity within
L178@P3: the study site.
L179@P3: Acoustic telemetry
L180@P3: Juvenile Lutjanus apodus (197.2  22.7 mm total
L181@P3: length [TL]  1 standard deviation [SD]) and
L182@P3: Haemulon plumierii (190.4  13.6 mm TL) were
L183@P3: captured via underwater hook and line or
L184@P3: trapped with a 30-m L 9 1 m H seine net at the
L185@P3: study site (Appendix S1: Table S1). Both species
L186@P3: were captured in the mangroves or on patch reefs
L187@P3: within 20 m from the mangrove edge. Our model
L188@P3: predator, Sphyraena barracuda (390.8  31.8 mm
L189@P3: TL), was captured with a seine net from the study
L190@P3: site. Vemco V8-4H transmitters (Vemco, Bedford,
L191@P3: Nova Scotia, Canada) were surgically implanted
L192@P3: into all three species: L. apodus (n = 10),
L193@P3: H. plumierii (n = 10), and S. barracuda (n = 5).
L194@P3: Each transmitter was inserted in the abdominal
L195@P3: cavity through a small incision between anal and
L196@P3: pelvic fins. Similar to Moulton et al. (2017), one or
L197@P3: two interrupted stitches with absorbable sutures
L198@P3: (4-0 Ethicon vicryl) were used to close the wound.
L199@P3: Post-operative fish were placed in a holding tank
L200@P3: with aeration for 15–30 min and then released at
L201@P3: capture sites. All transmitters were programmed
L202@P3: with a random delay of 80–160 s and tagging
L203@P3: occurred from 21 May to 26 May 2014. Total number of tagged animals released into the array was
L204@P3: restricted (n = 25) to minimize acoustic collisions
L205@P3: based on recommended maximum capacity of the
L206@P3: acoustic positioning system given our transmitter
L207@P3: programming (short delays = increased collisions), receiver spacing, high site fidelity of study
L208@P3: species, and limited seascape size.
L209@P3: An acoustic positioning system comprised of
L210@P3: 12 Vemco VR2W omnidirectional receivers was
L211@P3: deployed within the selected seascape, encompassing a detection area of approximately
L212@P3: 30,000 m2
L213@P3: . Acoustic receivers within the array
L214@P3: were closely spaced (~50 m) with overlapping
L215@P3: detection ranges, which allowed us to triangulate
L216@P3: fish positions (Dance and Rooker 2015). To minimize the effects of internal transmitter placement
L217@P3: on detection range (Dance et al. 2016), receiver
L218@P3: spacing was determined from a priori range testing using an internally tagged H. plumierii placed
L219@P3: at several locations within the study area. Twelve
L220@P3: synchronizing transmitters or sync tags (Vemco
L221@P3: V13-1H, 69 kHz) with a nominal delay of 600 s
L222@P3: (range: 500–700 s) were co-located with receivers
L223@P3: within the acoustic positioning system to synchronize the internal clocks of the VR2W receivers and act as reference tags. Acoustic receivers
L224@P3: were either attached to 2” diameter PVC poles
L225@P3: inserted in the sediment or in poles cemented
L226@P3: into cinder blocks (e.g., receivers in the channel).
L227@P3: The array was in place until 30 June 2014, and
L228@P3: the minimum duration of the tracking trial for
L229@P3: any tagged fish was 35 d (maximum = 41 d).
L230@P3: Dietary tracers
L231@P3: The potential carbon contribution of four primary producers (phytoplankton, seagrass, mangroves, and benthic microalgae [BMA]) was
L232@P3: investigated for L. apodus, H. plumierii, and
L233@P3: S. barracuda. Surface water samples for particulate organic matter (POM), a proxy for phytoplankton, were collected in 4-L containers and
L234@P3: vacuum-filtered (<130 kPa) immediately upon
L235@P3: returning to the laboratory onto precombusted
L236@P3: 0.7-lm GF/F filters, and then frozen (20°C).
L237@P3: Sediment collections of BMA were taken using a
L238@P3: ❖ www.esajournals.org 4 April 2018 ❖ Volume 9(4) ❖ Article e02200
L239@P3-4: ROOKER ET AL.grab sampler, and the vertical migration technique (Wells et al. 2008) was used to separate
L240@P4: BMA from the substrate. Benthic microalgae
L241@P4: were filtered and frozen for stable isotope analysis. Mangrove leaves and seagrass blades were
L242@P4: carefully collected by hand at the study site and
L243@P4: stored in ziplock bags in a cooler until returning
L244@P4: to the laboratory. This plant material was then
L245@P4: scraped with a spatula to remove all encrusting
L246@P4: organisms and epiphytic algae and stored frozen
L247@P4: (20°C). Lutjanus apodus, H. plumierii, and S. barracuda used for diet analysis were collected with
L248@P4: pole spears after the completion of the tagging
L249@P4: trial.
L250@P4: Samples from all primary producers and fishes
L251@P4: were thawed and then dried at 60°C for 24–48 h.
L252@P4: Dried filters for POM were packed into tin capsules. Muscle tissue from fishes and plant tissue
L253@P4: (blades, leaves) were dried and then powdered
L254@P4: using a mortar and pestle, and approximately
L255@P4: 1.0 mg was packaged in tin capsules. All samples
L256@P4: were analyzed for stable isotopes of carbon
L257@P4: (d13C) and nitrogen (d15N) at the Stable Isotope
L258@P4: Facility at the University of California at Davis,
L259@P4: CA, USA. Isotopic ratios are reported relative to
L260@P4: Vienna PeeDee belemnite for carbon and atmospheric N2 for nitrogen. Lipids were not
L261@P4: extracted from fish tissue; however, C:N ratios
L262@P4: were low (<4) across the size spectrum of fishes,
L263@P4: indicating a low lipid content and little influence
L264@P4: of lipids on fish tissue d13C values (Post et al.
L265@P4: 2007). Isotopic values are expressed using the
L266@P4: standard d notation, as parts per thousand (&).
L267@P4: Data analysis
L268@P4: Time-indexed, triangulated positions from the
L269@P4: acoustic positioning system were filtered by horizontal position error (HPE) following Dance and
L270@P4: Rooker (2015). Based on analysis of 12 in situ static transmitters within the array, we observed
L271@P4: that triangulated positions with HPE <12 generally correspond to positioning errors of <2 m. In
L272@P4: response, further analysis of position data was
L273@P4: limited to HPEs below this threshold. Also, positions obtained within the first 30 min of the fish
L274@P4: being released into the seascape were omitted to
L275@P4: minimize the effect of release location on resulting patterns of habitat use. The influence of time
L276@P4: of day on location in the seascape was investigated by partitioning triangulated positions
L277@P4: among day, night, and crepuscular (twilight)
L278@P4: periods. Given that the timing of sunrise and
L279@P4: sunset changed over the course of the trial, a
L280@P4: midpoint for sunrise and sunset between
L281@P4: observed times on 26 May and 26 June was used.
L282@P4: Periods 50 min before sunrise (05:52 h) and
L283@P4: 50 min after sunset (19:01 h) approximated the
L284@P4: beginning and end of twilight (civil and nautical)
L285@P4: and were used here to denote the pre-sunrise
L286@P4: and post-sunset twilight periods.
L287@P4: Triangulated positions were first classified to
L288@P4: habitat (mangrove, seagrass, patch reef, sand) to
L289@P4: estimate the proportion of detections for tagged
L290@P4: L. apodus, H. plumierii, and S. barracuda for each
L291@P4: habitat type within the seascape during three
L292@P4: time periods (day, night, and twilight) in ArcGIS
L293@P4: 10.22. Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was used to determine whether daily
L294@P4: occurrence within a specific habitat (percent of
L295@P4: detection by habitat by day) varied among the
L296@P4: three time periods (day, night, and twilight). Univariate contrasts (ANOVAs) based on daily percent occurrence by time period within each
L297@P4: habitat were also performed, but given that all
L298@P4: models were significant, only MANOVA results
L299@P4: are presented. The primary activity space of
L300@P4: S. barracuda (i.e., predator) was defined as the
L301@P4: 75% isopleth of a kernel density estimate (kde)
L302@P4: from all triangulated positions using Geospatial
L303@P4: Modeling Environment (GME, Beyer 2012). Initially, a mean 75% kde for S. barracuda was generated to define high use areas during each time
L304@P4: period; however, the number of triangulated
L305@P4: positions for this species was very low at night
L306@P4: and habitat use did not vary among the three
L307@P4: time periods. Thus, an overall activity space
L308@P4: (75% kde) was used to denote the high use area
L309@P4: of the model predator kde in our study area. In
L310@P4: turn, the spatial configuration of the predator
L311@P4: kernel density plot was then used to assess
L312@P4: whether habitat use and movements of L. apodus
L313@P4: and H. plumierii were linked to predator activity.
L314@P4: Although direct predation by S. barracuda on our
L315@P4: two potential prey species was not observed, predation on grunts and snappers by this predator
L316@P4: is known to occur (Randall 1967, Foss 2016). It
L317@P4: should also be noted that our model predator cooccurred with larger conspecifics in the seascape
L318@P4: and also used similar habitats (sand bottom in
L319@P4: the center of channel with higher current velocity) to other piscivores found in the Caribbean,
L320@P4: including jacks, groupers, and sharks (Bohlke
L321@P4: ❖ www.esajournals.org 5 April 2018 ❖ Volume 9(4) ❖ Article e02200
L322@P4-5: ROOKER ET AL.and Chaplin 1993). This indicates that the activity space derived for tagged S. barracuda
L323@P5: (<430 mm TL) likely applies to both larger conspecifics and other predators that frequent shallow water ecosystems in the Caribbean.
L324@P5: Locations of L. apodus and H. plumierii within
L325@P5: the seascape were further analyzed using Euclidean distance-based analysis (EDA; Conner et al.
L326@P5: 2003) to investigate the possible influence of predation threat on position and movement within
L327@P5: the seascape. This approach is commonly used to
L328@P5: evaluate habitat selectivity and important movement corridors in marine ecosystems (Furey
L329@P5: et al. 2013, Dance and Rooker 2015). Here, EDA
L330@P5: ratios were used to describe habitat use of L. apodus and H. plumierii relative to the high use areas
L331@P5: of a potential predator (i.e., 75% kde of S. barracuda). Euclidean distance-based analysis ratios
L332@P5: were calculated by first estimating distances of
L333@P5: all triangulated positions to the nearest border of
L334@P5: the predator activity space (i.e., 75% kde), with
L335@P5: all positions inside the predator kde assigned a
L336@P5: distance of 0. Distances of 1000 random positions
L337@P5: to the nearest border of the predator activity
L338@P5: space were also determined. For each individual,
